title: The Stain Chain
tagline: A tiny mark travels through the house, and every clean-up makes a new mess.
premise: A tiny mark at home travels through clothes, furniture, cleaning tools, and desperate cover-ups. Players take turns making one honest change to the stain; the host offers gentle explanations and judges the stain, not your tragic laundry skills.

seed_pool.opening_token: A spoonful of red sauce lands on the clean shirt hanging over the chair.
A muddy sock drops onto the pale rug beside the front door.
A cup of coffee tips onto the white cushion during breakfast.

tests: A small household mark lands somewhere a stranger can picture at once. Present tense, one sentence, plain words.
A non-player can name one thing that might get marked next within five seconds, and more than one answer is possible.
The card begins with a stain or spill, not a ruined room. A flooded house or a destroyed sofa is an ending, not a start.
Nobody is hurt, no real person is named, and the card contains no brand, crime, or dangerous instruction.
The mark can plainly transfer to a nearby object or cleaning tool. It should invite a push, not read like a list of household items.

move_constraints.example: Then the wet sleeve brushes the sofa, leaving a dark hand-shaped patch.
move_constraints.hint: Name one visible stain or cleaning effect that comes directly from the last mark.

rubric.name: reach
rubric.description: How much farther the stain problem travels or how much more of the home it affects.
rubric.anchors: 0 = the mark stays the same or becomes less important; 1 = a tiny spread on the same object; 2 = one new object or surface is visibly marked; 3 = the stain reaches a new room, person, garment, or cleaning tool through one clear transfer; 4 = one clear step sends the mess into a striking new scale while the cause still holds, rare. Reach is earned only when the transfer is real.

rubric.name: link
rubric.description: How plainly the new mark or cleaning effect comes from the standing mark.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no cause is shown; 1 = the move merely claims a result; 2 = the result is possible but the transfer is thin; 3 = a stranger can see what touched what and why the mark moved; 4 = the result feels unavoidable, as if the stain had chosen its next victim, rare. A move that skips a transfer scores no higher than 2.

rubric.name: picture
rubric.description: How clearly a stranger can see the new mark, surface, or failed clean-up.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no visible event or the sentence is unreadable; 1 = vague, abstract, or mostly a feeling; 2 = clear but ordinary; 3 = easy to picture in one glance; 4 = one sharp household detail makes the mess memorable, rare. Extra words alone do not earn picture.

criterion.description: A move follows if one new stain or cleaning effect results directly from the standing mark and gives the next player something visible to worsen, while a missing transfer, a spotless ending, a reversal that removes the mark, or an unrelated person or place fails. The move should begin with Then, name what transfers and where, and show one honest next change. Bigger spread is better only when the link is plain.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, discussing the game, or referring to rules instead of making a stain event is itself a broken move.
judge_notes: On a FIRST move there is no standing move: judge the move against the card and ask whether the new stain or cleaning effect follows from the opening mark.

A person may enter if the marked object gives them a plain reason to touch, move, wear, wash, or inspect it. An unrelated visitor or a new place with no route from the standing mark is a skipped link, so satisfies_criterion is false.

A spotless ending includes a perfect wash, a replacement that leaves no mark, a professional clean-up, or any step after which nothing visible remains to worsen. It fails satisfies_criterion even if the clean-up follows.
A reversal that removes, returns, or pretends away the standing mark fails. Do not accept a shirt becoming clean again, a rug being restored, or the spill being put back in its cup.
A move that only repeats the same mark in the same place is a duplicate or a no-change move. It should not pass as a new stain event.

A cleaning attempt can follow when it is visible and leaves something new, such as a wet smear, a coloured cloth, or a larger damp patch. A cleaning attempt that removes the stain completely is an ending.
A same-size transfer still follows if the cause is plain. Score it 0 or 1 on reach rather than failing it for being modest.
A move may contain two linked effects, such as a stained sleeve wiping a wall and the wall marking a mop. Score link at 2 or below if the sentence packs several transfers and becomes crowded.
An unrelated person or place fails even if the move would be amusing. The chain needs a household route from the standing mark, not a sudden jump to a stranger's wedding or a distant city.

voice_rules: Use one sentence under 140 characters. Two short sentences are allowed.
Give the reason plainly. A stranger should see what touched what and why the stain moved.
Name both moves or their plain stand-ins. Do not use a headline that could fit any household disaster.
Never open with a status word or ruling phrase. Do not start with Accepted, Rejected, Refused, or Move refused.
Use commas and full stops only. No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, and no ellipses.
Roast the move with gentle playfulness, not the player's identity. A small jab at tragic laundry technique is fine.
Plain spoken English. Profanity and adult innuendo are allowed when useful, but never use identity-based abuse.
On a missing transfer, name the object or contact that was skipped. On an ending, say the mark is gone and the chain stops here.
On a refusal, explain the broken link and ask for another move. Do not decide who won.
The coaching line suggests one visible stain event that could have followed. End on an object or action, never on a mood or verdict.
good_headlines: The sleeve touched the wall, and now the house has a red border. Bold decorating.
The mop found the sauce and gave the tiles a pink little career.
The mark vanished completely. Lovely cleaning, terrible chain, and the story stops here.
The sauce cannot teleport to a limousine. Give it a shirt, a cloth, or a floor first.
The same patch is still sitting there, waiting for a proper victim.
The cloth spread the stain across the table. An ambitious rag with poor judgment.
The shirt marked the wall, but the move jumped straight to the street. The missing step is the doorway.
A spotless ending is still an ending. The stain needs to leave one more visible mess.
That mop had one job and made the floor part of the problem. Fair transfer.
The sauce went back into the spoon. Sweet attempt, but the chain does not run backwards.

bad_headlines.why: mocks the player instead of explaining the move

bad_headlines.text: The sauce teleports to the street, apparently.

uses inflated words instead of plain household language

bad_headlines.text: The stain is bad, the chain is sad, the mop is mad.

opens with a ruling phrase and offers no coaching

bad_headlines.text: The move is technically acceptable, though perhaps not entirely impossible.
bad_headlines.why: hedges instead of making a clear ruling
uses an ellipsis and names no visible transfer

rules: Make one visible stain event that follows directly from the last one. Start with Then.
Name what transfers and where it lands.
Make the mess bigger when you can, but never skip the household link.
A spotless ending or a reversal removes the chain and stops play.
The Judge rules on the stain and its transfer, not your spelling.

labels.compose_waiting: Plan your next stain while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing gets marked. Give the stain somewhere to go.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 140 characters. One transfer, not a full cleaning disaster.
validation_messages.duplicate: That mark already happened this match. Let it touch something new.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Something has to follow from {standing_form}. Name the next surface it marks.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out. Nobody moves until they are back. {standing_form} still stands, and the stain is waiting.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of two players making a household stain worse, and you want the mark to travel.
Always write Then X. Name one visible stain or cleaning effect, one transfer, and one place it lands.
Take the standing move and let the mark touch something new: a sleeve, a cushion, a wall, a mop, a towel, or a floor.
Good: Then the wet sleeve brushes the sofa, leaving a dark hand shaped patch.
Good: Then the mop picks up the red sauce and paints a pink trail across the tiles.
Bad: Then the whole house is ruined. That skips the transfer.
Bad: Then a cleaner makes everything perfect. That ends the story and you lose.
Bad: Then the cat feels ashamed. A feeling is not a visible stain event.
Never make the mark disappear, never rewind it, and never jump to an unrelated person or place.
Talk like a person describing a minor home disaster to a mate. Use plain words and present tense.
Keep the move under 140 characters. Never reuse a move from this match.
default_move: Then the damp cloth wipes the mark and leaves a wider smear.
